task_title: Demonstration of Flight Characteristics at Various Configurations and Airspeeds
area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain power required and the two command regions across the speed range, fly the clean and landing configuration demonstrations from the right seat while you narrate them, and teach them: brief, demonstrate, supervise practice, and spot and fix the common errors.
why: This Task shows a learner, in their own airplane, how attitude, power, trim and control feel change from maneuvering speed down to the edge of the stall [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Mismanaged altitude and airspeed contribute to the three most common kinds of fatal accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]], and the trap at the slow end, needing more power to fly slower, is the one that catches pilots low on a power approach or climbing out of ground effect [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. As a flight instructor you must be able to give this kind of training, and the FAA asks you to stress that each airplane has its own flight characteristics [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]].

warmup: Think first: your learner holds altitude at best glide speed with a low power setting, then slows almost to the stall and finds that holding altitude now takes much more power. They ask: 'Why does slower need more power?' Then, with the power left alone, you lower the nose and the airplane settles into level flight at a faster speed. How would you explain, with one sketch and two sentences, why the same power holds level flight at two different speeds? And where in the traffic pattern will this matter to them?

key_terms.def: The rate the airplane loses energy to total drag at a given airspeed (drag times airspeed) [[24:104|AFH 4-18]]. In level flight it is the power you must set to hold altitude at that speed [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].
The rate of energy gain from the maximum thrust available at a given airspeed (thrust times airspeed) [[24:104|AFH 4-18]].
The lowest point on the power required curve, where the least power sustains level flight; the PHAK calls it the best endurance airspeed [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Holding altitude, a higher airspeed needs a higher power setting and a lower airspeed a lower one. Most climb, cruise and maneuvering is flown here [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].
The speeds between the minimum power required speed and the stall, where a lower airspeed needs a higher power setting to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].
The AOA and lift coefficient that give the most lift for the least drag; flown in steady flight, total drag is at its minimum [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]]. Best glide speed occurs here [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
Below L/DMAX, if the airspeed drops it may keep dropping unless the pilot reduces the AOA or adds power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
The maximum speed at which the limit load can be imposed by gusts or full deflection of the controls without structural damage. It is lower when the airplane is lighter [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
VLE is the maximum speed with the landing gear extended; VLO is the maximum speed for extending or retracting it [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
The highest speed allowed with the flaps in a prescribed extended position, because of air loads on the flaps [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. It is the top of the white arc [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

Reference landing speed, the final approach speed. For single-engine landings the AFH says to use the manufacturer's recommended airspeed, or 1.3 VSO if there is none [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]. Use the POH number when there is one.

The stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration (VSO) or in a specified configuration (VS1) [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100d]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100e]]; the bottoms of the white and green arcs [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

chunks.title: What this demonstration is and why we teach it

body.p: This Task is a guided tour of the airplane's speed range. You start at maneuvering speed, slow in steps to the edge of the stall, then accelerate again without touching the power, first clean and then in the landing configuration (AI.X.B.S4, S5). At each stop the learner sees, hears and feels what changes: attitude, power, trim, control feel and the stall warning. The ACS objective calls it the flight characteristics and power required at different airspeeds and configurations of the make and model you fly (AI.X.B).

AC 61-67C asks the flight instructor to stress that techniques differ between aircraft and that pilots should know the flight characteristics of each aircraft they fly [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]]. Its first stall training element, stall avoidance practice at slow airspeeds, is very close to this Task: slow to just above the stall with trim, hold heading and altitude with the stall warning on, show trim and rudder effects, then fly turns, climbs and descents at low airspeed [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]] [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a]].

bullets: Purpose for the learner: fly at low speeds and high AOA, and learn the feel, sound and visual cues of a regime where the controls respond less and altitude is harder to hold [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

Why it matters: reduced airspeed is normal in takeoffs, departures, approaches and landings, close to the ground [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Mismanaged altitude and airspeed contribute to loss of control, CFIT and approach and landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

How it differs from slow flight (AI.X.A): slow flight is flown without a stall warning, about 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. This Task goes all the way to the airspeed where any more AOA, load factor or power reduction would stall immediately, while you acknowledge the warning aloud (AI.X.B.S4c, S4d).
On the checkride: for single-engine airplanes the evaluator selects Task A (slow flight) or Task B (this Task) in Area X (CFI ACS Area X note).

chunks.title: Power required from cruise to the edge of the stall

body.p: Start with drag. Parasite drag rises with the square of airspeed. Induced drag rises with AOA and varies inversely with the square of airspeed, so as the airplane slows toward the stalling speed, total drag grows, mainly from the sharp rise in induced drag [[1:105|PHAK 5-8]]. Total drag is lowest at one speed, L/DMAX [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]]. Power required is drag times airspeed [[24:104|AFH 4-18]], and the minimum power and maximum endurance point is a different point from minimum drag [[1:105|PHAK 5-8]] [[1:266|PHAK 11-10]].

Walk the curve from cruise down (AI.X.B.K2). At cruise, high speed and low AOA, there is little or no excess power [[24:91|AFH 4-5]]. As you slow, power required falls to its lowest point. Below it, power required climbs again, and at low airspeeds near the stall or minimum controllable airspeed the power needed for steady, level flight is quite high [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

The ACS wording to use on the checkride: the minimum power required speed and "its role in differentiating the region of normal command and the region of reversed command on the power-required curve" (AI.X.B.K3). The PHAK says the same: reversed command is the band of speeds "between the speed for minimum required power setting and the stall speed (or minimum control speed)" [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]], and it calls that lowest point the best endurance airspeed [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. The AFH's own Figure 4-4 draws the backside and front-side line at the minimum power airspeed [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

head: Region
Speeds
Holding altitude, to fly slower you
Where the learner meets it
rows: Normal command
Above the minimum power required speed
Reduce power
Climb, cruise and most maneuvers [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]
Reversed command
From the minimum power required speed down to the stall
Add power
Low speed phases, such as a low-airspeed, nose-high power approach for a short-field landing [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]] [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]

body.p: Two points to teach. First, reversed command is about the power needed to hold altitude at each speed; the controls themselves do not reverse [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. Second, below L/DMAX the airplane is speed unstable: if turbulence takes a few knots off, the airspeed may keep decaying until the pilot reduces the AOA or adds power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

callout.text: Draw the curve on the whiteboard before the flight and mark where each stop will fall: maneuvering speed on the right, best glide in the middle, the edge of the stall at the far left. In flight, name each stop as you reach it. Application: every power setting the learner notes then lands on a point they can picture.

check.q: Your learner says, 'In reversed command the elevator and throttle swap jobs.' What definition do you give instead?
check.a: It is flight where, holding altitude, a higher airspeed needs a lower power setting and a lower airspeed needs a higher one [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. The AFH adds that below L/DMAX pitch becomes the more effective airspeed control [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

chunks.title: Load factor, weight, CG and the other relationships

body.p: Lift, AOA and load factor were taught in Principles of Flight (AI.II.D). Here, link each one to what the learner will see during this demonstration, and keep to the cause and effect the airplane can show.

Figure 4-5 shows why a bank costs power. In a bank the load factor rises, so you pull back to increase AOA; that raises induced drag and the power required at any given speed [[24:92|AFH 4-6]]. In the figure the curve for a higher load factor sits higher, so less excess power is left.

head: Factor
What changes
Source
rows: Lift and airspeed
At a constant AOA, lift varies with the square of airspeed; to hold altitude while slowing, the AOA must increase
Drag and AOA
At high AOA, small changes in AOA cause significant changes in drag
Angle of attack
A given airplane stalls at the same AOA regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude
Load factor
Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor; a level 60° bank is 2 G and raises the stall speed 41 percent
Power required
A level turn needs more AOA and so more induced drag; the extra thrust needed is proportional to the bank
Weight
More weight needs a higher AOA for the extra lift, so the stall speed rises
Center of gravity
Forward CG: higher stall speed and higher elevator forces. Aft CG: less elevator force to reach a high AOA, less control at slow speed, and a harder stall or spin recovery
Attitude
Nose-high at low speed, a vertical component of thrust helps support the airplane. A stall can happen in any attitude, so vision alone is not a foolproof cue
Yaw effects
Torque, slipstream and P-factor can give a strong left yaw; the closer to the 1G stall, the more right rudder is needed
Controllability
Less airflow over the control surfaces means larger movements for the same response, the 'mushy' feel
Stalls and spins
An airplane must be stalled and yawed to enter a spin; mishandled yaw at the stall makes a spin more likely

callout.text: Show the load factor effect at best glide speed, not at the edge. At the S4c airspeed any bank or pull is an immediate stall by definition (AI.X.B.S4c). Application: a shallow level turn at best glide speed shows the extra power needed on the tachometer with margin to spare.

check.q: Your learner loads the trainer near the forward CG limit. What two differences should they expect at the slow end?
check.a: A higher stall speed and higher elevator control forces [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]].

chunks.title: Pitch, power and trim across the speed range

body.p: Use the AFH energy language. The throttle controls total energy and the elevator distributes it between altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. To slow down at constant altitude, reduce the throttle and gradually pitch up just enough to hold altitude, retrimming as needed; to speed up at constant altitude, add throttle and gradually pitch down [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

head: Flight condition
Near cruise airspeed
At critically slow airspeed
rows: Level flight
Hold the level attitude with a light touch; trim off the pressures so little control force is needed [[24:69|AFH 3-8]] [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]
More power is needed to hold altitude as the airspeed nears the target; trim, or strong back pressure makes precise control difficult [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Turns
Back pressure to hold altitude, and power added to counter the loss of speed from drag, more in steeper banks [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
Power must be increased to hold altitude in turns [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; added load factor brings the critical AOA closer [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]
Climbs
Climb power set, airspeed held with the elevator, nose-up trim [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Climb and descend by adjusting power once stabilized; expect more yaw at high power and counter it with rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Descents
Reduce power as the descent is entered to hold the same airspeed [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]
Small pitch changes make large airspeed changes, so pitch controls airspeed and power the path [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]

body.p: The key shift: below L/DMAX, small pitch changes make disproportionately large changes in induced drag and airspeed, so pitch becomes the more effective airspeed control and power the effective path control [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. AC 61-67C puts it both ways: airspeed is controlled primarily by the elevator at a given configuration and power, and by power at a given configuration and AOA [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100b]].

Figure 4-12 is a good debrief tool. Its 'Cautions when very slow' column calls lower and very slow dangerous: apply full throttle and avoid pitching up, which adds drag on the backside of the curve [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. If even full throttle gives no excess power, the only recourse is to trade altitude for speed by pushing forward first, then advance the throttle [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

callout.text: Trim at every stop. Set the attitude first, hold it, then trim off the pressure; do not fly the airplane with the trim [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]. Have the learner say each trim change aloud so they notice how much nose-up trim the slow end takes.

check.q: In the AFH energy rules, what does the throttle do when you trade altitude for speed, as in S4e?
check.a: Rule 3: do not change the throttle at first, pitch down to trade altitude for speed, then adjust the throttle at the end as needed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

body.p: This element is about your airplane, so start with its POH and a checkout flight. The AFH says pitching moments from extending and retracting flaps, gear and other drag devices should be covered in any specific airplane checkout [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

bullets: Flaps increase both lift and induced drag at any given AOA, which allows a lower landing speed [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]]. Flap extension generally lowers the stall speed, which is why the white arc starts below the green arc [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100c]].
Up to about 15° of flap mainly adds lift with little drag, and the airplane tends to balloon; beyond 15° the drag rises sharply [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

Pitch change: flap camber gives a nose-down moment, but deflection beyond 15° can give a strong nose-up moment in some high-wing airplanes as downwash on the tail changes, so the result depends on the design. Be ready to retrim at every flap change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Gear and flaps add drag [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]]. When drag increases, the nose must come down to hold airspeed and the glide steepens [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Retracting flaps at low speed: anticipate the AOA change; abruptly raising the flaps in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
Power changes the stall speed too: in the PHAK sample table, wings level, power on stalls at a lower speed than power off in both configurations [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

body.p: Use the table in the brief. For this sample airplane, wings level and power off, gear and flaps down lowers the stall from 65 to 57 knots, and every column rises with bank [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. Your POH has its own table; the demonstration lets the learner see where those numbers fall on the dial.

callout.text: AC 61-67C asks you to demonstrate proper flap extension and retraction in level flight at low airspeed and to note the change in stall speed with flaps extended and retracted [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a]]. The landing configuration demonstration is the natural place.

check.q: In the PHAK sample table, how much do gear and flaps lower the wings-level, power-off stall speed?
check.a: From 65 to 57 knots, a drop of 8 knots [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

chunks.title: The airspeeds to know, and where to find them

body.p: Know every speed for the airplane you bring to the checkride, from its POH, and know which ones are on the dial. Airspeed indicators on small airplanes certificated after 1945 carry a standard color code; some important limits are not marked and are found on placards and in the AFM/POH [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

head: Speed
What it means
On the airspeed indicator?
Why it matters in this Task
rows: Design/operating maneuvering speed (VA, VO)

VA: the maximum speed at which the limit load can be imposed by gusts or full deflection of the controls without damage; lower at lighter weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. VO: a historical limit for certain airplanes, the maximum speed where full control excursion at any weight stays within the design limit load [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]
Not marked; placards and AFM/POH [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
The starting speed of both demonstrations, set for today's weight (AI.X.B.S4a, S5a)
Landing gear extended/operating speed (VLE, VLO)
VLE: maximum speed with the gear extended, a stability and controllability limit. VLO: maximum speed to extend or retract it, a limit for air loads on the mechanism [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]
Not marked; AFM/POH [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]
If applicable, slow to VLO before extending the gear (AI.X.B.S5b)
Flaps extended/operating speed (VFE)
The highest speed allowed with the flaps in a prescribed extended position, because of air loads on the flaps [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]
Top of the white arc [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
Limits flap extension in S5b and the acceleration in S5f
Best glide speed
The speed that gives the greatest distance for altitude lost in still air, at L/DMAX; a heavier airplane needs a higher speed for the same glide ratio [[24:83|AFH 3-22]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
The sources do not say; use the POH
The second stop of the clean demonstration (AI.X.B.S4b)
Reference landing speed (VREF)
Final approach speed. For single-engine landings the AFH says to use the manufacturer's recommended airspeed, or 1.3 VSO if there is none [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]
The sources do not say; use the POH
The target in the landing configuration (AI.X.B.S5c)
Stalling speeds (VSO, VS1)
VSO: stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration. VS1: the same in a specified configuration [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]
VSO bottom of the white arc; VS1 bottom of the green arc [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
A published 1G stall speed holds only in unaccelerated, coordinated flight at one weight and CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]

body.p: Teach what the arcs assume (AI.X.B.R1). In small airplanes VSO is the power-off stall speed at maximum landing weight in the landing configuration, and VS1 is usually the power-off stall speed at maximum takeoff weight, clean [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. At a lighter weight, with power on or in a turn, the real stall speed differs from the arc. In flight, have the learner note where the stall warning comes on compared with the arc.

callout.text: VA protects only against a single full control input in one axis. Operating at or below VA gives no structural protection against multiple full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]], and large alternating inputs can cause failure at any speed [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]].

check.q: The POH gives VA at gross weight, and today you are well below gross. What does that mean for the S4a entry speed?
check.a: VA is lower at a lighter weight, so use the POH value for today's weight, as the ACS says 'appropriate to the airplane's weight' (AI.X.B.S4a) [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

chunks.title: Airspeed indicators and stall warnings: range and limits

body.p: Airspeed indicators (AI.X.B.R5):

bullets: Installation and instrument errors can total several knots at some airspeeds and flap settings, and are generally greatest at low airspeeds; use the calibration chart [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

The color markings may be indicated or calibrated airspeed, and VSO and VS1 are defined as calibrated speeds [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. Application: the indicated speed at the edge of the stall may not match the bottom of an arc.
In uncoordinated flight the pitot-static instruments, especially the altimeter and airspeed indicator, are unreliable [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].
A blocked pitot tube or static port gives false airspeed; check the openings during the preflight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

body.p: Stall warning indicators:

bullets: Many stall warning devices alert the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. Certification allows the warning to come from aerodynamic buffet or from a device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
A stall warning system can fail; then use other cues such as aerodynamic buffet, loss of roll authority or inability to arrest a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
In some icing conditions a stall may come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]].
AOA indicators are limited by calibration techniques, unheated probes or vanes, the type of indicator, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

body.p: Unacknowledged stall warnings (AI.X.B.R6). In this Task the warning stays on while you hold the edge, and the ACS requires you to acknowledge it aloud (AI.X.B.S4d, S5e). That creates a trap: in normal flight, failure to respond to a stall warning is a listed common error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]], and the longer it takes to recognize an impending stall, the more likely a full stall [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. AC 61-67C's slow-airspeed practice also holds the warning on [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]], so the difference must be briefed.

callout.text: Application: brief it in plain words. 'In this demonstration we hold the horn on purpose, we call it out, and we leave when I say. Anywhere else, the horn means lower the nose now.' Never let the horn become background noise.

check.q: If the stall warning system fails, which other cues does the AFH tell the pilot to use?
check.a: Aerodynamic buffet, loss of roll authority and inability to arrest a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

chunks.title: Reversed command, the critical AOA and critically slow maneuvering

body.p: Reversed command and loss of control (AI.X.B.R3). The PHAK gives two examples your learners will meet. On a low-airspeed, nose-high power approach with a high sink rate, power may stop the descent; without more power the airplane would probably stall or be unable to flare, and lowering the nose alone gives a rapid sink [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. On a soft-field takeoff, climbing out of ground effect too slowly can leave the airplane unable to climb even at full power; the only recourse is to lower the nose and accept some altitude loss [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

The AFH shows the same path on its energy charts: from climbing, to no climb, to the stall horn, where power available is less than power required [[24:102|AFH 4-16]]. It names unstable or slow approaches, high-drag go-arounds with gear or flaps left down, and steep turns in the pattern as places this happens [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

bullets: Inadvertent exceedance of the critical AOA (AI.X.B.R4): a stall can happen at any airspeed, attitude and power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. The critical AOA is most often exceeded in three situations: low speed, high speed and turning [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

Maneuvering at critically slow airspeeds (AI.X.B.R9): at the S4c and S5d airspeed, any more AOA, load factor or power reduction gives an immediate stall by definition (AI.X.B.S4c). Application: no turns, no pulls and no power reductions while you hold it.
Abrupt or rough control movements in slow flight may result in a stall, and abruptly raising the flaps can cause one [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
Control effectiveness falls with airspeed, so larger movements are needed for the same response [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
Uncoordinated flight can create the potential for a spin [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]; a spin needs a stall plus yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Keep the ball centered.

callout.text: This is what the demonstration is for. Low and very slow, more pitch only adds drag; the fix is full power and, if that is not enough, less AOA first. Close to the ground there may not be room [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

check.q: On a soft-field departure your learner climbs out of ground effect too slowly, and the airplane will not climb at full power. What does the PHAK give as the only recourse?
check.a: Lower the pitch attitude to increase airspeed, which costs some altitude [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

chunks.title: Airspeed limits, the environment and traffic

body.p: Exceeding airspeed limitations (AI.X.B.R2) is most likely at the configuration changes and during the acceleration. Extend gear and flaps at speeds that keep you within the limits for extending them [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]: VFE protects the flaps from air loads and VLO the gear mechanism [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. Never let the airspeed reach the red line during practice stalls [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]], and avoid full or abrupt control movements at or above VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]].

callout.text: In S5f you lower the nose with the flaps fully down and the power unchanged. Application: watch the top of the white arc. The ACS asks for a faster airspeed, not one above VFE; level off before you reach it.

body.p: Environmental elements (AI.X.B.R7):

bullets: Turbulence: a vertical gust can cause a sudden, abrupt increase in AOA, and the airplane can stall at a significantly higher airspeed than in smooth air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. Below L/DMAX, a speed loss from turbulence may keep growing [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. Application: in rough air keep more margin at the slow end, or move the lesson.
Microbursts: downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots seriously degrade performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. At the slow end there is little excess power to absorb that.

High density altitude: performance decreases [[1:260|PHAK 11-4]] and the power available curve is lower [[24:101|AFH 4-15]]. Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].

body.p: Altitude and clearing (AI.X.B.S2, S3, R8). Pick an altitude that keeps the maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (AI.X.B.S2), the same minimum the AFH recommends for single-engine stall practice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] and AC 61-67C uses for stall demonstrations and slow flight [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]]. Add the altitude lost in S4e and S5f, measured on your own practice flights. Clear the area before the maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] and have the learner call 'clear' aloud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

Collision hazards: training airspace may be crowded, and haze and pollution aggravate the hazard [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Make the lookout a shared job; if learners believe the instructor does all the scanning, they never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Why is haze a special concern for this demonstration in a busy practice area?
check.a: Practice airspace can be crowded, and restricted visibility from haze aggravates the collision hazard, so both pilots share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

chunks.title: Fly it: the clean configuration demonstration

body.p: Fly it from the right seat and explain as you go, including the power settings and attitudes [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Here is the clean sequence with sample patter.

bullets: Setup (S2, S3): altitude chosen, area cleared with turns and callouts [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

Design/operating maneuvering speed (S4a): establish and maintain VA or VO for today's weight, level and trimmed. Describe pitch, power and trim: 'This power holds altitude at this speed, this is the attitude on the horizon, and the trim takes the pressure off.' [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]

Best glide speed (S4b): gear and flaps up, reduce power and raise the nose gradually to hold altitude as the airplane slows, retrimming [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. Hold best glide speed in level flight and read out the power setting: 'Best glide, level, this much power. Remember the number.' Best glide speed occurs at L/DMAX [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

Edge of the stall (S4c): keep slowing with more nose-up attitude, and add power as needed to hold altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Settle at the airspeed where any further increase in AOA or load factor, or reduction in power, would stall immediately. Hold it level and note airspeed and power: 'Slower than best glide, and it takes more power. That is reversed command.' [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]
Stall warning (S4d): verbally acknowledge each cue as it comes: 'Horn on, light buffet, mushy ailerons, lots of right rudder.' [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]

Accelerate (S4e): without changing the power setting, lower the nose and let the airplane accelerate until it is established in level flight at a faster airspeed. Note the new airspeed and the altitude lost. The AFH calls this trading altitude for speed with the throttle left alone [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]; on the backside, the push gives a brief energy-exchange descent toward the center of the power curve, where total drag is lower [[24:91|AFH 4-5]]. Application (your patter, not an AFH line): 'Same power, a faster level speed. We paid for it with altitude.'
Return to cruise (S4f): set cruise power, return to the altitude and heading the evaluator gave, and trim [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

head: Stop
Say and note
Standard (AI.X.B.S1, as appropriate)
rows: S4a maneuvering speed
Pitch, power and trim to hold altitude and airspeed
Altitude ±100 ft, airspeed +5/-0 kt, heading ±10°
S4b best glide

Altitude ±100 ft, airspeed +5/-0 kt, heading ±10°
S4c edge of the stall

Altitude ±100 ft, airspeed +5/-0 kt, heading ±10°

callout.text: Why S4e matters: on the backside, pushing forward gives a brief energy-exchange descent that accelerates the airplane toward the center of the power curve, where excess power appears [[24:91|AFH 4-5]]. It is the way out for an airplane stuck low and slow, and the learner has just seen it work without a power change.

check.q: Which numbers does the ACS have you note at the S4b, S4c and S4e stops?
check.a: S4b: the power setting at best glide. S4c: the airspeed and power setting at the edge, while acknowledging the stall warning. S4e: the new airspeed and the altitude lost (AI.X.B.S4b, S4c, S4d, S4e).

chunks.title: Fly it: the landing configuration demonstration

body.p: The landing configuration demonstration repeats the story with gear and flaps fully extended. The ACS sequence, with what to say:

bullets: Design/operating maneuvering speed (S5a): the same start as the clean demonstration: VA or VO for today's weight, describing pitch, power and trim to hold altitude and airspeed.

Limiting airspeeds and full extension (S5b): reduce power and slow at constant altitude. Extend the gear at or below VLO if it is retractable, and the flaps at or below VFE, in the steps your POH allows, retrimming after each change [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Name what the airplane does: 'First flaps, it wants to balloon; a little nose down. More flaps, more drag; more power.' [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]

Reference landing speed (S5c): with gear and flaps fully extended, slow to VREF or the speed the evaluator gives, hold it level and note the power setting. Without a manufacturer number, the AFH uses 1.3 VSO [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

Edge of the stall (S5d): with gear and flaps fully extended, slow to the airspeed where any further increase in AOA or load factor, or reduction in power, would stall immediately. Hold it level and note airspeed and power. Compare it with the clean edge; the flaps lowered the stall speed [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]].
Stall warning (S5e): verbally acknowledge every stall warning indication.

Accelerate (S5f): without changing the power, lower the nose, accelerate and re-establish level flight; note the new airspeed and altitude lost. VFE is the highest speed allowed with the flaps extended [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]; application: level off before you reach it.

Return to normal cruise (S5g): add power; as the airspeed increases, retract the flaps and the gear (if retractable) while anticipating the AOA change, retrim, and return to the evaluator's altitude and heading [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

body.p: Hold the S1 standards throughout, as appropriate: altitude ±100 feet, airspeed +5/-0 knots, heading ±10° (AI.X.B.S1). Application: expect different power numbers from the clean demonstration because of the extra drag; record your own airplane's values for your lesson plan.

callout.text: Raise the flaps smoothly and at a safe speed. Abruptly raising the flaps in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]], and AC 61-67C has you show learners how errors in flap retraction can cause a secondary stall [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200e]].

check.q: With full flaps at the edge of the stall, why must you watch the airspeed closely during S5f?
check.a: You accelerate with the flaps down, and VFE, the top of the white arc, is the highest speed allowed with the flaps extended because of the air loads on them [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]] [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

body.p: Teach it on the ground first. The AIH says progress on stalls through flight instruction alone is slower than when they are first discussed on the ground, and you should review the task before flight even if ground school covered it [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. Draw the power required curve and mark each stop; have the learner predict whether each stop needs more or less power than the one before.

body.p: AC 61-67C's slow-airspeed elements give you add-ons for later lessons [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]] [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a]]:

bullets: Trim: show the effect of neutral and full nose-up elevator trim at low airspeed [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]].
Yaw: note the left turning tendency, have the learner center the ball with right rudder, then release the rudder and let them watch the left yaw [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]].
Adverse yaw: at low airspeed, have the learner enter turns without the rudder pedals [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]].

Distractions: once the sequence is solid, add a task such as finding a heading on a chart or a 200-foot climb and descent; later, fly low airspeeds with the airspeed indicator covered at various flap settings [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a]].
Sight picture: early on, mark horizontal reference lines for the slow flight and cruise attitudes [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

body.p: Build it in blocks: clean before landing configuration, and the simple skill before the combined one [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. To check understanding rather than rote memory, change the starting speed or the flap setting and ask the learner to predict the power before setting it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Integrated flight instruction: introduce each maneuver with both outside and instrument references from the first time [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Here, link each attitude on the horizon to the tachometer and airspeed numbers the learner notes.

check.q: Your learner had stall ground school last month. Why does the AIH still say to talk through this Task on the ground before the flight?
check.a: Progress on stalls through flight instruction alone is slower than when they are also discussed on the ground, and the instructor should review the task before flight even after ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

body.p: No source lists errors for this Task by name. The table below is assembled from four AFH common error lists: slow flight [[24:117|AFH 5-12]], intentional stalls [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], straight-and-level flight [[24:70|AFH 3-9]] and descents [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Each error is on the cited list; the fixes cite the pages that teach them. On the checkride the evaluator may play a learner who makes these errors; you analyze and correct them (AI.X.B.S6).

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to adequately clear the area
Slowing starts with no turns or callouts
Clear before the maneuver and call 'clear' aloud [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]]
Inadequate back-elevator pressure as power is reduced
Altitude loss as the slowdown starts
Raise the nose gradually to hold altitude as the speed decays [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]
Excessive back-elevator pressure as power is reduced
A climb, then a rapid loss of airspeed
Smaller, gradual pitch changes matched to the deceleration [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Insufficient right rudder
Nose yaws left; ball not centered
More right rudder as speed falls and power rises [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Fixation on the flight instruments
Head inside, chasing the needles
Most attention outside, with brief instrument checks [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Failure to anticipate AOA changes as flaps move
Balloon or sink at each flap change
Expect the change, adjust pitch and retrim [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Inadequate power management
Altitude lost at the edge because power was not added
Add power as the speed nears the target; slower than minimum power speed needs more [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]
Failure to properly trim the airplane
Strong back pressure, wandering pitch
Trim at every stop; do not fly with the trim [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]
Failure to respond to a stall warning
The warning is not called aloud, or is ignored outside the briefed hold
Acknowledge it aloud; outside the hold, reduce AOA at once [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Chasing the flight instruments (the airspeed indicator)
Pitch oscillates as the learner reacts to every needle movement
Set the attitude on the horizon, then cross-check [[24:70|AFH 3-9]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Inadvertent accelerated stall from pulling too fast on the controls
A quick pull at the edge turns the buffet into a stall break
Small, smooth inputs [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; if it stalls, reduce AOA first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]

body.p: Application, not on any AFH list: in S4e and S5f a learner who lowers the nose too little stays slow on the backside. The fix follows from the AFH energy rules: pitch down enough to trade altitude for speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

Tell a misunderstanding from a motor skill problem by having the learner think aloud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. A learner who expected less power at the slow end needs the curve again on the ground; one who knew the answer but lagged needs more practice.

callout.text: Safety permitting, let the learner go part of the way into an error, such as a slow altitude loss at the edge, and find the fix; learners who seldom correct an error learn the maneuver poorly [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. At the edge of the stall, 'part of the way' is very short.

check.q: At the best glide stop the pitch keeps oscillating as your learner reacts to every movement of the airspeed needle. Name the listed error and the fix.
check.a: Chasing the flight instruments, here the airspeed indicator [[24:70|AFH 3-9]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Set the attitude on the horizon and hold it, then cross-check the instruments [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].

scenario.title: First flight in a retractable trainer on a hot, bumpy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. A commercial learner with 180 hours is flying the school's retractable-gear single for the first time and wants the flight characteristics demonstration. The airport elevation is 2,400 ft, the highest terrain in the practice area is 2,900 ft, it is a hot afternoon with cumulus and light to moderate bumps below the bases, and the practice area is busy. With two aboard the airplane is about 300 lb below gross. On the ramp the learner says, 'I know the speeds; they're on the dial.'

questions.q: The learner says they know the speeds from the dial. What do you check first, on the ground?
questions.a: Which limits are not on the dial: VA, VLO and VLE come from placards and the AFM/POH [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]], and VA is lower at today's lighter weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Also what the arcs assume: VSO is the power-off stall at maximum landing weight in the landing configuration [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

questions.q: On your practice flight the clean push (S4e) cost 250 ft. What is the lowest entry altitude here?
questions.a: 2,900 + 1,500 + 250 = 4,650 ft MSL, so the maneuver stays no lower than 1,500 ft AGL (AI.X.B.S2) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The 250 ft is your own measured number, not a source value.

questions.q: It is bumpy at the planned altitude. How does that change the slow end?
questions.a: A vertical gust can abruptly raise the AOA and stall the airplane at a higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]], and below L/DMAX a speed loss may keep decaying [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. The AIH has you coach the learner through the risk and its mitigation, which can mean changing the lesson plan [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Application: climb to smoother air if you can, or keep more margin at the slow end.

questions.q: How does the hot afternoon change the picture at the slow end of the power curve?
questions.a: The power available curve sits lower at high density altitude [[24:101|AFH 4-15]], so there is less excess power at every speed, and the AFH's energy-depletion example ends with the airplane unable to climb and the stall horn sounding [[24:102|AFH 4-16]]. Brief that the edge of the stall will need more of the available power today.

questions.q: During S5b the learner reaches for the gear handle 20 knots above VLO. What do you say, and why?
questions.a: Wait: slow to VLO first. VLO is the limit for air loads on the gear mechanism during extension or retraction [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]], and gear and flaps are extended only at speeds within their limits [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

questions.q: At the landing configuration edge, the horn has sounded for 20 seconds and the learner has stopped calling it. What do you do?
questions.a: Have them acknowledge it aloud, as the ACS requires (AI.X.B.S5e), and keep watching the traffic, since the slow segment is long [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. In the debrief, separate the briefed hold from normal flight, where failure to respond to a stall warning is a common error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

skills.do: Conduct and explain both demonstrations while "maintaining altitude ±100 feet, airspeed +5/-0 knots, heading ±10°, and specified bank angle ±5°, as appropriate", narrating each power setting, attitude and trim change as you fly.
skills.practice: Fly the whole sequence with another instructor applicant, talking aloud the entire time, and record the power at each stop for your airplane [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: Select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed "no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL)" and explain how you added the altitude lost in S4e and S5f.
skills.practice: Before each flight, write terrain elevation plus 1,500 ft plus your measured altitude loss on your kneeboard [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Clear the area before starting, with callouts, and keep the lookout going through the long slow segments.
skills.practice: Use the same clearing turns every time and call 'clear' aloud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

skills.do: Fly the clean demonstration in the ACS order: maneuvering speed for the weight with pitch, power and trim described; best glide speed noting power; the edge of the stall noting airspeed and power while acknowledging the warning; the push to a faster level airspeed on the same power, noting airspeed and altitude lost; then cruise at the evaluator's altitude and heading.
skills.practice: Practice the S4e push at altitude until your altitude loss is consistent, and sketch your numbers on a power required curve [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

skills.do: Fly the landing configuration demonstration: maneuvering speed, gear and flaps extended within VLO and VFE, VREF noting power, the edge with the warning acknowledged, the acceleration without exceeding VFE, then cleanup and return to cruise.
skills.practice: Rehearse the flap steps and retrim at each; know VFE and VLO without looking them up [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]].

skills.do: When the evaluator, acting as a learner, makes errors such as not adding power at the edge or a timid push in S4e, name the error, explain its cause and give the fix.
skills.practice: Have a colleague fly the sequence with planted errors from the AFH lists while you call them out [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

quiz.q: In the PHAK's example of a slow, nose-high power approach in the region of reversed command, what happens if the pilot only lowers the nose to regain flying speed, without adding power?
options: The airplane accelerates and settles level on the front side
The sink stops as soon as best glide speed is reached
A rapid sink rate and a matching loss of altitude
The airspeed decays further as the nose comes down
quiz.why: Merely lowering the nose without power in that situation results in a rapid sink rate and loss of altitude; power may stop the descent [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

quiz.q: What does the PHAK call the lowest point on the power required curve?
options: Best rate of climb airspeed
Best glide airspeed
Best endurance airspeed
Design maneuvering speed
quiz.why: The lowest point is the speed at which the lowest brake horsepower sustains level flight, the best endurance airspeed [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

quiz.q: Which limiting speed is shown on a standard single-engine airspeed indicator?
options: Design maneuvering speed (VA)
Landing gear operating speed (VLO)
Landing gear extended speed (VLE)
Maximum flap extended speed (VFE)
quiz.why: VFE is the top of the white arc [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. VA, VLO and VLE are not marked; they are on placards and in the AFM/POH [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

quiz.q: Why is VLO a separate limit from VLE?
options: VLO limits air loads on the mechanism as the gear moves
VLO applies only above 10,000 feet in turbocharged models
VLO is a stability and control limit with gear down
VLO protects the tires from overheating on landing
quiz.why: VLO is about air loads on the operating mechanism during extension or retraction; VLE is about stability and controllability with the gear down [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say certification standards permit as an airplane's required stall warning?
options: An aural horn or light only, never buffet
Pre-stall buffet or a stall warning device
A stick shaker, required in every airplane
An AOA indicator that senses flap position
quiz.why: Certification standards permit the required stall warning either through the airplane's inherent aerodynamic qualities (pre-stall buffeting) or through a stall warning device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, which flap range mainly adds lift with little drag and tends to make the airplane balloon?
options: Up to about 15°
Beyond 15°
Full flaps only
None; flaps add only drag
quiz.why: Flap deflection of up to 15° primarily produces lift with minimal drag, with a tendency to balloon; beyond 15° drag rises sharply [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

quiz.q: Your airplane's VA is 99 knots at gross weight, and today it is light. For S4a you should:
options: Use the lower VA the POH gives for the weight
Use a faster speed, since lighter airplanes have margin
Use 99 knots, since VA is fixed by the airframe
Use VNO, since VA is only for turbulence
quiz.why: VA is lower when the airplane is lighter [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]], and the ACS asks for maneuvering speed appropriate to the airplane's weight (AI.X.B.S4a).

quiz.q: What does AC 61-67C say altitude does to an airplane's indicated stall speed?
options: Raises it about 2 percent per 1,000 ft
Raises it only above 10,000 ft
Lowers it as density altitude rises
Little or no effect
quiz.why: Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed; true airspeed is higher in thin air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].

quiz.q: Per AC 61-67C, how does stall speed change with load factor?
options: In proportion to the load factor
In proportion to the square of the load factor
In proportion to the square root of the load factor
It does not; only the AOA changes
quiz.why: Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

quiz.q: Where does the AFH say best glide speed occurs?
options: At the bottom of the green arc
At the lowest point of the power required curve
At 1.3 times VSO
At the highest lift-to-drag ratio (L/DMAX)
quiz.why: Best glide airspeed occurs at the highest lift-to-drag ratio, L/DMAX [[24:83|AFH 3-22]]. The lowest point of the power required curve is best endurance [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

final_quiz.q: At the S4c stop your learner needs much more power to hold altitude than at best glide, and asks if the tachometer is wrong. Your explanation?
options: No; slower than minimum power speed needs more power
Yes; induced drag falls as you slow, so power should too
No; the propeller just loses efficiency at high rpm
Yes; carburetor ice has cut the power at low airspeed
final_quiz.why: Below the minimum power required speed, a lower airspeed needs a higher power setting to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. Induced drag rises as airspeed falls [[1:105|PHAK 5-8]].

final_quiz.q: During S4e you lower the nose with the power unchanged; the airplane accelerates and settles level, faster and 120 ft lower. What do you tell the learner?
options: The push stalled the tail, which dropped the nose and altitude
It traded altitude for speed, toward the center of the curve
Drag rose at the faster speed, so the airplane had to sink
Lowering the nose added power by unloading the propeller
final_quiz.why: With the throttle left alone, pitching down trades altitude for speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. On the backside the push gives a brief energy-exchange descent that accelerates the airplane toward the center of the power curve, where total drag is lower [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

final_quiz.q: At the S5d edge with full flaps, your learner raises all the flaps at once 'to clean up quickly.' What is the main risk?
options: A stall, from the sudden loss of lift at low speed
Exceeding VFE as the airplane accelerates at once
Structural damage to the flap tracks from air loads
Engine overheating from the sudden drag change
final_quiz.why: Abruptly raising the flaps in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; AC 61-67C shows how flap retraction errors cause a secondary stall [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200e]].

final_quiz.q: Acting as your learner, the evaluator holds the S4c airspeed in a 15° bank 'to show some maneuvering.' What do you say?
options: Fine; the ACS allows ±5° from whatever bank you pick
Fine; with the ball centered the stall speed is unchanged
No; at that speed any added load factor stalls it
No; banks are allowed only in the landing configuration
final_quiz.why: S4c is the airspeed where any further increase in load factor gives an immediate stall (AI.X.B.S4c). A level bank needs more AOA [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]], and load factor raises the stall speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH gives no VREF. VSO is 48 knots. What target does the AFH suggest for S5c, unless the evaluator specifies one?
options: 48 knots, which is VSO
About 62 knots, 1.3 VSO
About 67 knots, which is 1.4 VSO
Best glide speed
final_quiz.why: With no manufacturer's speed, the AFH uses 1.3 VSO on final [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]: 1.3 x 48 = 62.4, about 62 knots. 1.4 VSO (1.4 x 48 = 67.2) is the AFH base leg target [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner calls the bottom of the white arc 'the stall speed' and expects the S5d stall exactly there today, with power on and the airplane light. What do you teach?
options: Correct; the arc is valid for every weight and power
The arc is VFE; the stall is at the bottom of the green arc
The arc is VS1 in the landing configuration
The arc is VSO under set conditions; today's will differ
final_quiz.why: The white arc's lower limit is VSO, the power-off stall at maximum landing weight in the landing configuration [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. A published 1G stall speed holds only at one weight and CG in unaccelerated, coordinated flight [[24:118|AFH 5-13]], and power on lowers it [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

final_quiz.q: Using the AFH energy table, your learner is lower than desired and very slow, near the ground. What is the AFH guidance?
options: Apply full throttle and avoid pitching up
Pitch up to stop the descent, then add power
Hold the attitude and add power gradually
Reduce power to idle and glide at best glide
final_quiz.why: The very slow column calls this dangerous: apply full throttle and avoid pitching up, which adds drag on the backside of the power required curve [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

final_quiz.q: At the landing configuration edge, the evaluator as learner adds full power before lowering the nose for S5f. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing; power first is always the correct order
S5f is flown without any change in power
Full power with flaps down always exceeds VNO
Adding power at the edge is prohibited by the POH
final_quiz.why: The ACS says to lower the pitch and accelerate without changing the power setting (AI.X.B.S5f). The AFH calls this trading altitude for speed with the throttle left alone [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: You fly the clean demonstration in moderate turbulence. Which risk does AC 61-67C point to at the S4c stop?
options: Turbulence lowers the indicated stall speed
Turbulence moves the CG aft during each gust
A gust can abruptly raise AOA and cause a stall
Gusts matter only above maneuvering speed
final_quiz.why: A vertical gust can cause an abrupt increase in AOA, so the airplane can stall at a significantly higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

final_quiz.q: You want an example from the AFH of where a learner can reach the slow edge of the energy envelope at low altitude. Which one does it list?
options: A stabilized final approach flown at 1.3 VSO
A go-around with the gear or flaps left down
Level cruise at maneuvering speed in smooth air
A cruise climb at VY with the flaps retracted
final_quiz.why: The AFH lists unstable or slow approaches, high-drag go-arounds where the pilot neglects to raise the gear or flaps, and steeper-than-normal turns in the traffic pattern [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

final_quiz.q: In the AFH energy rules, which inputs move the airplane to a slower airspeed at constant altitude?
options: Less throttle and pitch down to hold the airspeed
More pitch first with no throttle change, then retrim
More throttle and a gradual pitch down
Less throttle, gradually more pitch to hold altitude
final_quiz.why: To slow down at constant altitude, reduce the throttle and gradually pitch up just enough to maintain the path, retrimming as needed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's POH lists VO rather than VA for the S4a and S5a entry speed. How does the AFH describe VO?
options: The maneuvering speed at maximum gross weight only, used for flight in turbulence
A historical limit where full control travel at any weight stays within limit load
The highest speed for operating the flaps in any position during the approach
The best glide speed at maximum landing weight, used for emergency descents
final_quiz.why: VO is a historical operating limitation for certain airplanes: the maximum speed at which full control excursion at any weight stays within the design limit load factor [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: In S5b your learner extends 30° of flap in one step at VFE, and the high-wing trainer pitches up and balloons. What do you teach?
options: Nothing; flaps always pitch the nose down
Use full flaps only above VFE to avoid the balloon
Expect a pitch change; use steps and retrim
Flaps have no effect on pitch in high-wing designs
final_quiz.why: Flaps can balloon the airplane and, beyond 15°, give a nose-up moment in some high-wing airplanes; extend them in increments and retrim at each change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

takeaways: This Task tours the speed range: maneuvering speed, best glide, the edge of the stall, then a push to a faster speed on the same power, clean and in the landing configuration (AI.X.B.S4, S5).
The minimum power required speed divides normal from reversed command; below it, slower needs more power to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].
Below L/DMAX, pitch is the more effective airspeed control, power controls the path, and the airplane is speed unstable [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Low and very slow: full power and less AOA, not more pitch [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].
Know which speeds are on the dial and which come from the POH, and set VA for today's weight [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
Hold the stall warning only when briefed, and say it aloud; anywhere else the warning means act [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
No lower than 1,500 ft AGL plus your measured altitude loss, and clear the area first (AI.X.B.S2, S3).
cfi_notes: Where reversed command starts, quoted. ACS K3: the minimum power required speed and "its role in differentiating the region of normal command and the region of reversed command on the power-required curve." PHAK: reversed command is the band "between the speed for minimum required power setting and the stall speed (or minimum control speed)" [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. AFH slow flight text: "When flying at speeds below L/DMAX, more power is required to fly even slower" [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. These differ, because minimum power and minimum drag occur at different points [[1:105|PHAK 5-8]]. Teach the ACS and PHAK line (the AFH's own Figure 4-4 also divides the curve at the minimum power airspeed [[24:91|AFH 4-5]]), and explain the AFH 5-10 shorthand if a learner has read it.

The PHAK adds that reversed command 'does not imply that a decrease in power produces lower airspeed' [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. Learners often find that line confusing; teach the definition by the power needed to hold altitude at each speed.

The ACS S1 altitude tolerance of ±100 feet applies 'as appropriate,' while S4e and S5f deliberately lose altitude and ask you to note it. The ACS does not say how the two fit; agree with the evaluator before the flight that the loss is part of the maneuver.
For single-engine airplanes, Task A (slow flight) and Task B are alternatives; the evaluator picks one (CFI ACS Area X note). Prepare both.

AC 61-67C 200a is the FAA's closest description of how to give this lesson: hold heading and altitude with the warning on, show trim, rudder and adverse yaw, demonstrate flap changes, then add distractions and a covered airspeed indicator [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a]] [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a]].

The AFH landing chapter gives 1.3 VSO for final approach when the manufacturer gives no speed [[24:174|AFH 9-3]] but does not use the term VREF there; the AFH defines VREF (normally 1.3 VSO) only in its multiengine chapter [[24:250|AFH 13-1]]. Use the POH number when there is one.
VO is in the ACS wording, but the AFH calls it a historical limitation that applies to certain airplanes only [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Check which one your POH publishes.

If your airplane has an AOA indicator, get training on it from someone knowledgeable before you teach with it [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]; this demonstration is a good time to show how the display moves across the speed range.
Record your airplane's power settings, airspeeds and altitude loss at each stop during your own practice. No source can give them, and they make your ground brief concrete.
gaps: Power settings, airspeeds and altitude loss at each stop are specific to the airplane; no source gives them. Measure them and record them.
The sources do not say whether best glide speed or VREF is marked on the airspeed indicator; use the POH.
Partial flap speeds and any separate flap operating speed come only from the POH; the PHAK defines VFE for a prescribed extended position [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]].
No source gives a common error list written for this Task; the error table is assembled from the AFH slow flight, intentional stall, straight-and-level and descent lists.
How much altitude to allow for S4e and S5f is not given anywhere; it depends on how far the nose is lowered and on the airplane.

activities.title: True or false: airspeed indicators and stall warnings
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Airspeed indicator errors are generally greatest at low airspeeds.
cards.why: True. Installation and instrument errors can total several knots and are generally greatest at low airspeeds [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

cards.s: In a skid, the airspeed indicator stays accurate as long as the wings are level.
cards.why: False. In uncoordinated flight the pitot-static instruments, especially the altimeter and airspeed indicator, are unreliable [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

cards.s: A stall warning system can fail, so other cues still matter.
cards.why: True. If it fails, use buffet, loss of roll authority or inability to arrest a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

cards.s: In this Task, the stall warning at the S4c stop means you must lower the nose at once.
cards.why: False for this demonstration: you hold the airspeed in level flight and acknowledge the warning aloud (AI.X.B.S4c, S4d). In normal flight, failure to respond to a stall warning is a common error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

cards.s: Airspeed indicator color markings are always in indicated airspeed.
cards.why: False. The markings may be IAS or CAS [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]].

cards.s: Some AOA indicators do not account for flap setting.
cards.why: True. Some indicators take flap position into account, but not all [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

activities.title: Numbers for your brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your POH lists VSO as 52 knots and gives no VREF. Using the AFH rule of 1.3 VSO, what VREF do you target in S5c?
Same airplane: the AFH suggests about 1.4 VSO on the base leg. What speed is that?
PHAK stall speed table, gear and flaps up, wings level: 54 knots power on and 65 knots power off. How many knots lower is the power-on stall speed?
items.why: 65 - 54 = 11 knots [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. Expect the stall warning to come at a different airspeed with power on than the green arc suggests.

items.q: An older airplane with no published VA stalls at 58 knots. Using the PHAK rule of thumb of about 1.7 times the normal stalling speed, estimate VA.
items.why: 58 x 1.7 = 98.6, about 99 knots [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. The PHAK calls this a guide only; use the manufacturer's VA.

items.q: PHAK table, gear and flaps down, power off: 57 knots wings level and 81 knots at 60°. Divide 81 by 57. (A 2 G turn predicts the square root of 2, 1.41.)
items.why: 81 / 57 = 1.42, within 0.01 of the square root of 2 (1.414), since stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

activities.title: CFI checkride: the evaluator plays your learner
activities.intro: You are the CFI applicant in the right seat. The evaluator plays a private pilot learner flying the clean demonstration in a fixed-gear trainer. Terrain tops out at 1,400 ft MSL and you are level at 3,500 ft.

steps.s: The 'learner' sets 120 knots for S4a: 'VA is 105 at gross, but I like a margin above it.' Your call?
options: Slow to VA for today's weight; above VA full control inputs can overstress the airplane
Fine; faster gives more stall margin
Use VNO instead, since it is marked
Skip S4a and start at best glide
steps.why: VA is the maximum speed for full control deflection without damage and is lower at lighter weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]; do not use full or abrupt control movements above it [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]]. The ACS asks for maneuvering speed appropriate to the weight (AI.X.B.S4a).

steps.s: Below best glide the 'learner' keeps raising the nose with the power unchanged, and the altitude starts to drop. What do you coach?
options: Lower the nose to hold altitude
Retrim nose-down
Reduce power to slow faster
Add power: below minimum power speed, slower needs more
steps.why: In the region of reversed command a lower airspeed needs more power to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]; inadequate power management is a listed error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

steps.s: At the edge the horn is on, the 'learner' says nothing, and the airspeed drifts 2 knots below the target. What now?
options: End the lesson and return to land
Have them call the warning aloud and ease the nose down to regain the target; the tolerance is +5/-0
Add full power and climb away
Accept it; 2 knots is within tolerance
steps.why: The airspeed tolerance is +5/-0 knots (AI.X.B.S1), and the warning must be acknowledged verbally (AI.X.B.S4d). Below L/DMAX a little less pitch is the effective airspeed correction [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

steps.s: For S4e, the 'learner' lowers the nose and adds power at the same time. Your correction?
options: Leave the power alone; the point is a faster level speed on the same power
Reduce power to idle to see the glide
Good; that minimizes altitude loss
Raise the flaps first
steps.why: The ACS says without changing the power setting (AI.X.B.S4e). The AFH calls this trading altitude for speed with the throttle left alone [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]; the push moves the airplane toward the center of the power curve [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

steps.s: After S4e you are at 3,280 ft. The evaluator asks for cruise at 3,500 ft, heading 090. What do you do?
options: Dive to cruise speed, then zoom up
Stay at 3,280 ft; the loss was expected
Cruise power, climb to 3,500 ft on heading 090, trim
Extend flaps to climb more steeply
steps.why: S4f asks for normal cruise at the evaluator's altitude and heading (AI.X.B.S4f). To climb, increase throttle so thrust exceeds drag and pitch up to hold speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].
